question: we got the excavator picking pipe with a choker on the bucket hook, does that put it under the crane rules?
gold_answer: No. Excavators (along with power shovels, wheel loaders, backhoes, loader backhoes and track loaders) are excluded from Subpart CC, even when they use chains, slings or other rigging to lift suspended loads.

key_quote.text: This machinery is also excluded when used with chains, slings or other rigging to lift suspended loads.

question: Driver drops off sheetrock with his knuckle boom truck and sets the bundles up on the 2nd floor deck with the forks on the end of the boom. Is he exempt from the crane standard or not?
gold_answer: He is excluded only if the truck crane has a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device. Moving building supply sheet goods or packaged materials from the truck onto a structure with a fork/cradle at the boom tip counts as material delivery. The exclusion is lost if the crane holds or stabilizes the material while it gets attached.

key_quote.text: using a fork/cradle at the end of the boom, but only when the truck crane is equipped with a properly functioning automatic overload prevention device

question: lumber yard knuckle boom is delivering the roof trusses and the guy wants to just set them up on the walls for us while he's here. thats still just a delivery right?
gold_answer: No. The material delivery exclusion does not apply when the articulating/knuckle-boom crane handles prefabricated components, and roof trusses (wood, cold-formed metal, steel or other material) are named as examples. Setting the trusses is covered by Subpart CC.

key_quote.text: Precast concrete members or panels, roof trusses (wooden, cold-formed metal, steel, or other material)

question: if i put a hook and winch atachment on the forklift to swing loads around does the crane standrd aply or is forklifts exempt
gold_answer: Forklifts (powered industrial trucks) are normally excluded. The exception is when the forklift is set up to hoist and lower (with a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load. In that setup it is covered by Subpart CC.

key_quote.text: Powered industrial trucks (forklifts), except when configured to hoist and lower (by means of a winch or hook) and horizontally move a suspended load.

question: Our all-terrain crane is rigged with a luffing jib and tower attachment. Do we follow the tower crane rules for it?
gold_answer: No. Under the definitions, a mobile crane configured with a luffing jib and/or tower attachment is not considered a tower crane.

key_quote.text: Mobile cranes that are configured with luffing jib and/or tower attachments are not considered tower cranes under this section.

question: digger derrick setting power poles and augering the holes is that covered by subpart CC or not
gold_answer: Yes, it is excluded from Subpart CC when augering holes for electric or telecom line poles, placing and removing the poles, and handling associated materials to be installed on or removed from them, or when doing any other work subject to Subpart V. To be eligible, use in Subpart V work must comply with all of Subpart V, and use in telecom service construction work must comply with all of § 1910.268.

key_quote.text: digger-derrick use in work subject to subpart V of this part must comply with all of the provisions of that subpart

expert_review.why: Whether the exclusion applies depends on full compliance with Subpart V or 1910.268, and that has to be judged in the field.

question: mechanic truck with the little crane on the back pulling an engine out of the dozer on site do the crane rules apply what if he uses it to set some rebar bundles
gold_answer: Pulling the engine is excluded because a mechanic's truck with a hoisting device is not covered when used for equipment maintenance and repair. Setting rebar is not maintenance or repair, so service/mechanic trucks with a hoisting device are covered by Subpart CC for that work.

key_quote.text: Mechanic's truck with a hoisting device when used in activities related to equipment maintenance and repair.

question: Who counts as the 'controlling entity' under the crane standard?
gold_answer: It is an employer that has overall responsibility for the construction of the project, meaning its planning, quality and completion. That can be a prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager or any other legal entity.

key_quote.text: an employer that is a prime contractor, general contractor, construction manager or any other legal entity which has the overall responsibility for the construction of the project

question: when we jump the tower crane up a few more sections is that considered erection or something else
gold_answer: It is erection. For tower cranes, 'erecting and climbing' replaces 'assembly', and raising the crane's height is an erection process whether it is built to full height at the start or climbed in stages.

key_quote.text: Regardless of whether the crane is initially erected to its full height or is climbed in stages, the process of increasing the height of the crane is an erection process.

question: Two things: (1) does the crane standard still apply when we hang a magnet or a man basket off the crane, and (2) what about a rig where we're just lifting with a chainfall?
gold_answer: (1) Yes. The standard applies to covered equipment used with attachments, crane-attached or suspended, including magnets and personnel platforms. (2) No. Machinery that hoists using a come-a-long or chainfall is excluded.

question: what about cherry pickers and scissor lifts, crane rules?
gold_answer: No. Machinery originally designed as vehicle-mounted aerial devices for lifting personnel, and self-propelled elevating work platforms, are excluded from Subpart CC.

key_quote.text: Machinery originally designed as vehicle-mounted aerial devices (for lifting personnel) and self-propelled elevating work platforms.

question: We built our own crane barge in house. What makes it a 'floating crane' vs a land crane on a barge, and is there a term for one we built ourselves?
gold_answer: A floating crane/derrick is designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other flotation. A land crane/derrick was not originally designed that way. A floating crane designed and built by an employer for its own use is called 'employer-made equipment'.

key_quote.text: designed by the manufacturer (or employer) for marine use by permanent attachment to a barge, pontoons, vessel or other means of flotation

question: Railroad crane working on mainline track. Do we still have to do the ground conditions section (1402)?
gold_answer: No, if certain conditions are met. Section 1926.1402 does not apply to cranes designed for railroad track when used on track that is part of the general railroad system regulated by the FRA under 49 CFR part 213, and the track complies with applicable FRA requirements.

key_quote.text: Section 1926.1402 does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks, when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation

expert_review.why: Whether a given track is part of the general railroad system and meets FRA requirements has to be decided case by case.

question: tree service is bringing a crane in to take down a big oak on the lot, crane standard cover that?
gold_answer: Subpart CC lists tree trimming and tree removal work as excluded from its coverage.

expert_review.why: The exclusion is one line, and whether other OSHA rules cover crane-assisted tree removal is outside this text.

question: what does the ground gotta be like before we can set up the crane, is there a rule or just eyeball it
gold_answer: You can't assemble or use the equipment unless the ground is firm, drained and graded well enough that the manufacturer's specs for support and level are met, using supporting materials like mats, blocking or cribbing if needed.

key_quote.text: The equipment must not be assembled or used unless ground conditions are firm, drained, and graded to a sufficient extent

question: We're setting up in a wetland on marsh buggies. The ground's soaked and there's no way to drain it. Does that automatically stop us?
gold_answer: No. The requirement that the ground be drained doesn't apply in marshes/wetlands. The ground still has to be firm and graded enough, with supporting materials such as marsh buggies, to meet the manufacturer's specs for support and level.

key_quote.text: The requirement for the ground to be drained does not apply to marshes/wetlands.

question: GC has the as-builts showing an old septic tank and a gas line right where we wanna put the outriggers. Do they have to tell us, or is that on us to find?
gold_answer: The controlling entity has to tell the equipment user and the operator where hazards under the set-up area are (voids, tanks, utilities) if those hazards show up in documents it has, on site or off site, such as site drawings, as-builts or soil analyses, or if it otherwise knows about them.

key_quote.text: Inform the user of the equipment and the operator of the location of hazards beneath the equipment set-up area (such as voids, tanks, utilities)

question: who has to do the ground prep if theres no GC or controling entity on the job
gold_answer: If there's no controlling entity, the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange the needed ground preparations must make sure they're provided.

key_quote.text: the employer that has authority at the site to make or arrange for ground preparations needed to meet paragraph (b) of this section

question: operator walks the setup area and says the dirt is too soft for the crane what's supposed to happen next
gold_answer: If the operator (or the A/D director) decides the ground conditions aren't adequate, that person's employer has to talk with the controlling entity about the ground preparations needed so the requirements can be met, using suitable supporting materials if necessary.

key_quote.text: that person's employer must have a discussion with the controlling entity regarding the ground preparations that are needed

question: Does the ground-conditions section in Subpart CC apply to a locomotive crane working on railroad track?
gold_answer: Not when it's a crane designed for railroad tracks, used on tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation regulated by the FRA under 49 CFR part 213, and those tracks meet the applicable FRA requirements. On any other track, the ground-conditions section still applies.

key_quote.text: This section does not apply to cranes designed for use on railroad tracks when used on railroad tracks that are part of the general railroad system of transportation

expert_review.why: Whether a particular track (for example plant or industrial spur track) counts as part of the general railroad system takes interpretation.

question: can we use our own company assembly procedure instead of the manufacturers? and does it matter if were rigging with synthetic slings
gold_answer: Yes, you can use employer procedures, but only if the employer can show they meet § 1926.1406, and you still have to follow every applicable manufacturer prohibition. If you use synthetic slings for A/D rigging, you must follow the manufacturer's procedures.

key_quote.text: The employer must follow manufacturer procedures when an employer uses synthetic slings during assembly or disassembly rigging.

question: If it's just me putting the jib on by myself, do I need any special qualification?
gold_answer: Yes. When only one person does the assembly/disassembly, that person has to meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person, and is treated as the A/D director.

key_quote.text: Where the assembly/disassembly is being performed by only one person, that person must meet the criteria for both a competent person and a qualified person.

question: A/D director's done this same boom setup a hundred times. Does he still have to go through the procedures right before we start?
gold_answer: Normally the A/D director has to review the procedures immediately before A/D starts. That review isn't required if the director understands the procedures and has already applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment, including any accessories.

key_quote.text: unless the A/D director understands the procedures and has applied them to the same type and configuration of equipment (including accessories, if any)

question: Halfway through teardown we get a new guy, and one of my hands switches from pinning to tag lines. What do I need to go over with them, and do I have to do it again for the guy switching jobs?
gold_answer: Yes, both. The A/D director must make sure each crew member understands their tasks, the hazards of those tasks, and the hazardous positions or locations to avoid. This applies before A/D starts, before a crew member takes on a different task, and when new personnel are added during the operation.

question: crew guy needs to climb under the counterweight where i cant see him during assembly what do we both have to do
gold_answer: Before he goes to an out-of-view spot in, on, under or near the equipment or load where he could be hurt, he has to tell the operator. Once you know he's there, you can't move any part of the equipment or load until you're told, through a pre-arranged communication system, that he's in a safe position.

key_quote.text: the operator must not move any part of the equipment (or load) until the operator is informed in accordance with a pre-arranged system of communication that the crew member is in a safe position

question: Tight site, and the only way to knock the boom pins out on this lattice crawler is to stand under the boom. Is that ever allowed?
gold_answer: Normally no one may be under the boom, jib or other components while pins are being removed. The exception applies only if the employer shows that site constraints require it. Then the A/D director must put procedures in place that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize how long and how much people are exposed under the boom.

key_quote.text: the A/D director must implement procedures that minimize the risk of unintended dangerous movement and minimize the duration and extent of exposure under the boom

expert_review.why: Whether site constraints really 'require' someone under the boom, and whether the procedures are adequate, are judgment calls.

question: During lattice boom assembly we're gonna hold the boom up with the boom hoist brake while guys work on it. Anything we have to do first, and what if the brake won't hold?
gold_answer: Every time you're going to rely on the boom hoist brake to stop boom movement, you have to test it first to see if it's enough. If it isn't, use a boom hoist pawl, another locking or back-up braking device, or some other way to prevent dangerous boom movement, such as blocking or an assist crane.

key_quote.text: the brake must be tested prior to such reliance to determine if it is sufficient to prevent boom movement

question: Setting lattice boom sections on cribbing during assembly with an assist crane. What are the rules on the blocking, and do the assist crane's loads need checking first?
gold_answer: The blocking's size, amount, condition and stacking method must be enough to carry the loads and keep things stable. It must also be placed so it protects the equipment's structural integrity and prevents dangerous movement and collapse. The loads on the assist crane at each phase must be verified under § 1926.1417(o)(3) before assembly starts.

key_quote.text: the loads that will be imposed on the assist crane at each phase of assembly/disassembly must be verified in accordance with § 1926.1417(o)(3) before assembly/disassembly begins

question: how much boom can we hang out cantilevered when we're pinning in sections? the manual for this old lattice crane is long gone
gold_answer: You cannot go past the manufacturer's limit on how much boom can be supported only by cantilevering. If the manufacturer's limits aren't available, a registered professional engineer familiar with that type of equipment must set the limit in writing, and that limit cannot be exceeded.

key_quote.text: Manufacturer limitations on the maximum amount of boom supported only by cantilevering must not be exceeded.

question: if we dont use the manufactuer's assembly procedure and write our own, who has to write it and what does it have to cover
gold_answer: Employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person. They must prevent unintended dangerous movement and collapse of any part of the equipment, provide adequate support and stability of all parts, and position employees so their exposure to unintended movement or collapse is minimized.

key_quote.text: Employer procedures must be developed by a qualified person.

question: what do we do with the shipping pins and straps after we pull them can we just leave them sitting on the boom
gold_answer: Reusable shipping pins, straps, links and similar items must be removed. Once removed they must be stowed or stored so they are not a falling object hazard, so leaving them loose on the boom is not acceptable.

key_quote.text: Once they are removed they must either be stowed or otherwise stored so that they do not present a falling object hazard.

question: Can we leave the jib on the crane while it's driving piles, or does it have to come off?
gold_answer: It has to come off. Equipment used for pile driving must not have a jib attached during pile driving operations.

key_quote.text: Equipment used for pile driving must not have a jib attached during pile driving operations.

question: tight site, can only get the outriggers out about halfway on one side. ok to make the pick like that?
gold_answer: Only if the manufacturer's procedures allow it. Outriggers must be fully extended, or, if the manufacturer's procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart (for example, using the chart for that partial extension).

key_quote.text: The outriggers or stabilizers must be either fully extended or, if manufacturer procedures permit, deployed as specified in the load chart.

question: on a locomotive crane do the outriggers have to lift it off the wheels like a truck crane? and what if we pick without the outriggers at all
gold_answer: No. The rule that outriggers must take the weight off the wheels does not apply to locomotive cranes; when using outriggers or stabilizers to handle loads, you follow the manufacturer's procedures. When lifting without outriggers or stabilizers, you must meet the manufacturer's procedures for truck wedges or screws.

key_quote.text: When lifting loads without using outriggers or stabilizers, the manufacturer's procedures must be met regarding truck wedges or screws.

question: stabilizers vs outriggers.. do stabilizers have to take the tires off the ground too? and does somebody have to watch them go down
gold_answer: No. The requirement to set outriggers so the equipment weight comes off the wheels does not apply to stabilizers. Each outrigger or stabilizer must be visible to the operator or a signal person while it is extended and set.

key_quote.text: This provision does not apply to stabilizers.

question: where exactly r we supposed to put the cribbing under the outriggers, can it go under the beam itself
gold_answer: Blocking goes only under the outrigger or stabilizer float/pad of the jack. If the outrigger or stabilizer has no jack, it goes under the outer bearing surface of the extended beam. The blocking must also meet the requirements of 1926.1404(h)(2) and (h)(3). Also, if floats are used, they must be attached to the outriggers or stabilizers.

key_quote.text: Be placed only under the outrigger or stabilizer float/pad of the jack

question: We're taking a boom section out to shorten the stick. The pendants are still tight. Can my guys start knocking out pendant pins or the pins on sections between the pendant attachment and the crane body?
gold_answer: No. Pendant pins can't be removed, even partly, while the pendants are in tension. Top or bottom pins on boom sections between the pendant attachment points and the crane body also can't be removed, even partly, while the pendants are in tension.

key_quote.text: None of the pins in the pendants are to be removed (partly or completely) when the pendants are in tension.

question: derrick boom is laid down with the tip section sitting on cribbing. can we pull the pins on the middle sections now
gold_answer: No. While the boom is held up by the uppermost section resting on the ground or another support, none of the top or bottom pins on sections between the uppermost section and the crane/derrick body may be removed, even partly.

key_quote.text: when the boom is being supported by the uppermost boom section resting on the ground (or other support)

question: taking off the cantilevered piece out past the pendant points, when can we pull the top pins on it
gold_answer: Top pins on boom sections in the cantilevered portion being removed (ahead of the pendant attachment points) can't be removed, even partly, until that cantilevered section is fully supported.

key_quote.text: are to be removed (partly or completely) until the cantilevered section to be removed is fully supported.

question: During assembly, who's allowed to do the rigging, and what special rules apply if we're using synthetic slings instead of wire rope?
gold_answer: A qualified rigger must do the rigging used for assembly/disassembly. Synthetic slings must be protected from abrasive, sharp or acute edges and from configurations that reduce rated capacity (such as distortion or localized compression), and the sling manufacturer's instructions, limitations, specifications and recommendations must be followed. Protection for wire rope slings is covered in 1926.251(c)(9).

key_quote.text: The rigging work is done by a qualified rigger.

question: how close can i get the stick to a 138kv line if were going by table A
gold_answer: 138 kV is in the 'over 50 to 200 kV' row of Table A, so the minimum clearance distance is 15 feet.

key_quote.text: over 50 to 200 | 15

question: Utility says the line is exactly 200 kV. Is that 15 ft or 20 ft on Table A? It's right on the edge.
gold_answer: 15 feet. Under the Table A note, the number after 'to' is included in that row, so 'over 50 to 200' covers 200 kV. The 20-foot row starts above 200 kV.

key_quote.text: The value that follows “to” is up to and includes that value.

question: We're putting the crane together next to some overhead lines. What do we have to figure out before assembly, and what are our choices if we could end up near them?
gold_answer: Before assembly or disassembly, the employer must determine whether any part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging) could get closer than 20 feet to a power line in the direction or area of assembly. If so, the employer must use one of three options: (1) have the utility confirm the line is deenergized and visibly grounded at the worksite, (2) keep 20 feet of clearance using the paragraph (b) measures, or (3) keep Table A clearance using the paragraph (b) measures.

key_quote.text: could get, in the direction or area of assembly/disassembly, closer than 20 feet to a power line during the assembly/disassembly process

question: can we lay out and pin the lattice boom sections on the crawler under the distribution line if we keep table A distance
gold_answer: No. During assembly or disassembly, no part of the crane, load line or load, whether partly or fully assembled, may be below a power line. The only exception is when the employer has confirmed that the utility has deenergized the line and visibly grounded it at the worksite. Keeping Table A distance does not make it allowed.

key_quote.text: is allowed below a power line unless the employer has confirmed that the utility owner/operator has deenergized and (at the worksite) visibly grounded the power line

question: During assembly near a line, is a flagged warning line enough as our extra measure? And is the warning line handled the same way once we start making picks?
gold_answer: Yes: during assembly/disassembly, an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs with flags or similar markings, in the operator's view, can be the one required additional measure if it is effective in preventing encroachment (a planning meeting is also required, and any tag lines used must be nonconductive). No, operations differ: under Option 2 or 3 the warning line is mandatory at 20 ft or the Table A distance respectively, plus at least one measure from 1926.1408(b)(4), and if the operator can't see the line, that must include a dedicated spotter plus one of the other (b)(4) measures.

key_quote.text: The measure selected from this list must be effective in preventing encroachment.

expert_review.why: Compares how the warning line is treated in assembly versus operations, and 'effective' is a judgment call.

question: operator cant see the warning line from the cab bc of a building in the way, what do we gotta do
gold_answer: If the operator can't see the elevated warning line, you must use a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator. You must also use one of the other measures: a proximity alarm, a range control warning device, a range-limiting device, or an insulating link.

key_quote.text: If the operator is unable to see the elevated warning line, a dedicated spotter must be used

question: Can an insulating link on the hook count as the encroachment measure? Does that work both for assembly and for regular picks?
gold_answer: During operations, yes. An insulating link/device installed between the end of the load line (or below) and the load is one of the allowed (b)(4) measures, used along with the required warning line. It is not on the list of additional measures for assembly/disassembly in 1926.1407(b)(3), so it can't serve as the assembly measure.

key_quote.text: An insulating link/device, as defined in § 1926.1401, installed at a point between the end of the load line (or below) and the load.

expert_review.why: The answer relies on the insulating link being left off the assembly list rather than an explicit ban.

question: how long does the power company have to give us the voltage if we want to go by the table
gold_answer: When the employer uses Option (3) (Table A clearance), the utility owner/operator must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the request.

key_quote.text: must provide the requested voltage information within two working days of the employer's request

question: knuckle boom truck settin up under a line thats way up there. when is it ok to work under it without getting it killed
gold_answer: For articulating or extensible booms, work below an energized line is allowed when the uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom fully extended at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the line, or more than the Table A distance below it. Otherwise the line must be deenergized and visibly grounded, unless another exception applies (subpart V work, or infeasibility plus 1926.1410).

key_quote.text: with the boom in the fully extended position, at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line

question: What is the exception for operating a fixed-length lattice boom crawler below an energized power line?
gold_answer: For non-extensible booms, the ban on working below a line does not apply if the employer shows that the uppermost part of the equipment, with the boom at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the line, or more than the Table A distance below it.

key_quote.text: with the boom at true vertical, would be more than 20 feet below the plane of the power line

question: Do the electrocution warning stickers have to go on the outside of a tower crane, or only in the cab?
gold_answer: At least one electrocution hazard warning must be posted conspicuously in the cab where the operator can see it. The requirement for at least two warnings on the outside of the equipment does not apply to tower cranes or overhead gantry cranes.

key_quote.text: at least one electrocution hazard warning conspicuously posted in the cab so that it is in view of the operator and (except for overhead gantry and tower cranes) at least two on the outside of the equipment

question: We're near a 400 kV transmission line. What's the trigger distance instead of 20 ft, and what's the Table A distance?
gold_answer: For lines over 350 kV up to 1,000 kV, 50 feet replaces 20 feet wherever 20 feet appears, including the trigger distance and the Option (2) clearance. Table A gives 25 feet for over 350 to 500 kV.

key_quote.text: wherever the distance “20 feet” is specified, the distance “50 feet” must be substituted

question: if the boom hits a hot line what are we suposed to tell the operater about staying in the cab vs jumping out
gold_answer: Operators must be trained that staying inside the cab is important for their safety. They should leave only if there is an imminent danger of fire, explosion or another emergency that requires it. Training must also cover the safest way to evacuate equipment that may be energized, the danger of touching the equipment and the ground at the same time, and step potential.

key_quote.text: remaining inside the cab except where there is an imminent danger of fire, explosion, or other emergency that necessitates leaving the cab

question: the lines look like theyve got coating on em, can we treat them as insulated
gold_answer: No. Power lines are presumed uninsulated unless the utility owner/operator, or a registered engineer who is a qualified person in power transmission and distribution, confirms the line is insulated. They are also presumed energized unless the utility confirms they are deenergized and visibly grounded.

key_quote.text: Power lines are presumed to be uninsulated unless the utility owner/operator or a registered engineer who is a qualified person with respect to electrical power transmission and distribution confirms that a line is insulated.

question: What counts as the work zone for the power line check if we don't set any boundaries? And who has to be in the planning meeting?
gold_answer: Without marked boundaries (flags or range limit devices) that the operator is prohibited from crossing, the work zone is the area 360 degrees around the equipment out to its maximum working radius. When Option 2 or 3 precautions apply, the planning meeting must include the operator and the other workers who will be in the area of the equipment or load.

key_quote.text: the area 360 degrees around the equipment, up to the equipment's maximum working radius

question: setting steel near a radio tower and the load is picking up a charge, whats required
gold_answer: When the equipment is close enough to a transmitter or communication tower for a charge to be induced in the equipment or materials, either the transmitter must be deenergized, or the equipment must be electrically grounded and any tag lines used must be nonconductive.

key_quote.text: The equipment must be provided with an electrical ground.

question: moving the hydro across the site no load, boom down, there's a 13.8kv distribution line we gotta drive under. how much clearance do i need to keep
gold_answer: For travel with no load, Table T requires a minimum clearance of 6 feet for lines over 0.75 kV up to 50 kV, so a 13.8 kV line needs 6 feet. The boom/mast also has to be lowered far enough to keep that clearance, and you have to account for how speed and terrain make the equipment move.

key_quote.text: over .75 to 50 | 6

question: Do I need a spoter when were just driving the crane under lines with nothing on the hook? Lines are pretty high but itll be close-ish
gold_answer: Yes, if any part of the equipment will get closer than 20 feet to the power line while traveling. The dedicated spotter has to be in continuous contact with the driver/operator, be positioned to effectively gauge the clearance, use communication equipment where necessary, and give the operator timely information.

key_quote.text: If any part of the equipment while traveling will get closer than 20 feet to the power line, the employer must ensure that a dedicated spotter who is in continuous contact with the driver/operator is used.

question: We have to reposition the crane after dark and the route goes under a set of lines. Beyond the usual stuff, what else is required for night travel?
gold_answer: At night or in poor visibility, on top of the normal travel requirements (boom lowered, Table T clearances, accounting for speed and terrain, and a spotter if closer than 20 ft), the power lines must be lit up or located some other way, and a safe path of travel must be identified and used.

key_quote.text: The power lines are illuminated or another means of identifying the location of the lines is used.

question: walking the crawler with a load on the hook under some lines, pick and carry. can i just use the travel table T distances
gold_answer: No. Table T and § 1926.1411 cover only travel with no load. Traveling with a load falls under § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever applies, plus § 1926.1417(u).

key_quote.text: Equipment traveling on a construction site with a load is governed by § 1926.1408, § 1926.1409 or § 1926.1410, whichever is appropriate, and § 1926.1417(u).

question: What is the minimum clearance distance required while traveling with no load beneath a 500 kV transmission line, and how does that change for a line above 1,000 kV?
gold_answer: A 500 kV line falls in the over 345 to 750 kV band, so the clearance is 16 feet. For lines over 1,000 kV, Table T sets no number: the distance is set by the utility owner/operator or by a registered professional engineer who is a qualified person in electrical power transmission and distribution.

key_quote.text: over 345 to 750 | 16

question: GC wants us to set something inside the Table A distance to an energized line. is that even allowed and what do we have to prove first before any of the planning stuff
gold_answer: It is prohibited unless the employer can show every requirement in § 1926.1410 is met. The first two are: (1) the work can't feasibly be done without breaching the Table A distance, and (2) after consulting the utility owner/operator, it isn't feasible to deenergize and ground the line or to relocate it. After that come the clearance determination, a planning meeting, documented procedures, and the rest of the section.

question: Two-part question on a job where we're working closer than Table A: how far out do the barricades around the crane have to be, and what if there's a building in the way?

question: running the knuckle boom off the belly box remote standing on the ground, close to hot lines under a 1410 plan. anything special for me as the operator
gold_answer: Yes. question: our boom truck has a range limiter. on a job inside table A do we have to use it or is the spotter enough
gold_answer: If the equipment has a device that automatically limits range of movement, it must be used. It has to be set so that no part of the equipment, load line or load (including rigging) breaches the minimum clearance distance set under § 1926.1410(c). question: For a line that has auto reclosers, what has to happen to them before we start working inside Table A? And who decides the actual clearance we hold?
gold_answer: Before work begins, the automatic reclosing feature must be made inoperative if the device's design permits. The minimum clearance distance is set by the power line owner/operator or by a registered professional engineer qualified in power transmission and distribution. They must consider on-site factors such as atmospheric conductivity, stopping time, wind, line sway and lighting.

question: halfway thru the pick near the lines the spotter loses comms and the plan clearly isnt working. what are we supposed to do, can we just finish the lift
gold_answer: No. If a problem comes up carrying out the procedures, or they prove inadequate to prevent electrocution, the employer must safely stop operations. Before resuming, the employer must either develop new procedures or have the utility owner/operator deenergize and visibly ground, or relocate, the line. The one designated person directing the procedures also has authority to stop work at any time.

question: utility crew with a digger derrick doing subpart V work inside table A — do they still need the elevated warning line and insulating link like a regular crane job
gold_answer: It depends first on the task: digger derricks augering holes for electric or telecom line poles, placing or removing those poles, or handling associated pole materials are excluded from Subpart CC (§ 1926.1400(c)(4)), and other rules govern that work. For Subpart V work that 1410 does cover, the elevated warning line/barricade (d)(3) and insulating link/device (d)(4)(i) requirements don't apply. question: how long do we gotta hang onto the monthly inspection sheets before we can toss em
gold_answer: The employer that does the monthly inspection must document the items checked and results, plus the inspector's name, signature and date. It must keep that record for at least three months.

question: For the annual crane inspection, what has to go on the paperwork, how long is it kept, and who gets to see it?
gold_answer: The record must show the items checked, the results, and the name and signature of the inspector with the date. The employer that conducted the inspection must keep it for at least 12 months. During that time it must be available to everyone who does inspections under 1926.1412.

question: crane been sitting in the yard since june its october now, its going back out on a construction job. do we need to do anything special before we fire it up and use it

question: does the shift inspection have to be all done befor we start pickin or can we finsh it durring the shift? and who has to do it
gold_answer: A competent person must start the visual inspection before each shift the equipment will be used. It may be finished before or during that shift.

question: do I have to boom down for the daily walkaround?
gold_answer: No. The shift inspection is visual, and booming down or taking components apart is not required. The exception is when the visual inspection or trial operation shows that further investigation needing those steps is necessary.

question: We shock loaded the hook this morning when a rigging hang-up let go, and the LMI showed it probably went over the chart. The super wants to keep working since nothing looks bent. What do we have to do?

For any deficiency, the qualified person must immediately determine whether it is a safety hazard (out of service until corrected, except for temporary alternative measures under 1926.1416(d) or 1926.1435(e)) or, though not yet a hazard, needs monitoring, in which case it must be checked in the monthly inspections.

question: When a repair has been made to a crane's braking system and the manufacturer provides no applicable criteria for that repair, what is the qualified person required to do before the crane goes back into service?
gold_answer: The qualified person must decide whether a registered professional engineer is needed to develop criteria. If not, the qualified person develops the criteria; if so, an RPE develops them. The qualified person then checks the repair against those criteria and functionally tests the repaired parts and any affected components. The crane can't be used until the inspection shows the criteria are met.

key_quote.text: If an RPE is not needed, the employer must ensure that the criteria are developed by the qualified person.

expert_review.why: Whether an RPE is needed is left to the qualified person's judgment.

question: just finished pinning the lattice stick together on the crawler, who's gotta sign off before we make the first pick and what are they checking it against
gold_answer: When assembly is finished, a qualified person must inspect the crane to make sure it is configured to the manufacturer's equipment criteria. If no manufacturer criteria exist, the criteria must be developed by the qualified person or, when needed, an RPE. The crane can't be used until the inspection shows it meets the applicable criteria.

key_quote.text: the equipment must be inspected by a qualified person to assure that it is configured in accordance with manufacturer equipment criteria

question: We run a locomotive crane on a mainline track that's under FRA. Does our shift inspection have to cover the rails, rail clamps and the track bed?
gold_answer: No. The shift-inspection items for rails, rail stops, rail clamps and supporting surfaces don't apply when the tracks are part of the general railroad system of transportation regulated by FRA under 49 CFR part 213. The same exclusion covers ground conditions for those tracks and their underlying support.

question: annual inspector found some wear that isn't dangerous yet. do we have to park the crane or what
gold_answer: The qualified person must decide right away whether the deficiency is a safety hazard. If it is not yet a hazard but needs watching, the employer must make sure it is checked in the monthly inspections. Only a deficiency judged a safety hazard requires taking the crane out of service until corrected, unless temporary alternative measures under 1926.1416(d) or 1926.1435(e) are used.

question: is cracked outrigger pads on the boom truck something the yearly inspection is supposed to catch
gold_answer: Yes. The annual/comprehensive inspection by a qualified person must check outrigger or stabilizer pads/floats for excessive wear or cracks.

question: On the truck crane annual, what are they looking for on the hydraulic cylinders, and how do they check the relief valves?
gold_answer: Cylinders are checked for: drifting from fluid leaking across the piston, leaks at rod seals and welded joints, scores/nicks/dents on rods, significant dents in the barrel, and loose or deformed rod eyes and connecting joints. Relief valves are checked for failure to reach correct pressure, and the manufacturer's pressure-check procedure must be followed if one exists.

question: we bolted on an aftermarket load hook block setup that ups the capacity, approved and everything. can we just go to work with it
gold_answer: No. After a modification affecting safe operation or capacity, a qualified person must inspect the equipment before initial use. question: manual says to inspect the hoist brake every week but osha only says monthly. which one do we go by
gold_answer: Follow the manufacturer. Any manufacturer inspection procedure related to safe operation, such as braking systems, that is more comprehensive or more frequent than 1926.1412 must be followed.

question: how many broken wires in the hoist line before i gotta pull it? regular running rope not the rotation resistant stuff
gold_answer: For running wire rope, six randomly distributed broken wires in one rope lay, or three broken wires in one strand in one rope lay, is a Category II deficiency. Operations using the rope are prohibited until the employer complies with the rope manufacturer's removal criterion (or a different one the manufacturer approved in writing for that rope), the rope is replaced, or, if the damage is localized, the rope is severed and only the undamaged portion is used (no splicing, and two wraps must remain on the drum at the lowest load and/or boom position).

question: broken wire limit on roation resistent rope?? is it diffrent from normal rope

question: Doing the walkaround on our lattice boom crawler and found a couple broken wires on a boom pendant right up by the socket. How many broken wires are allowed on pendants, and does it matter if they're at the end fitting?
gold_answer: Yes, location matters. question: how much can the rope diameter shrink before its a problem i mic'd it and its under nominal

question: We brushed a hot line yesterday and the load line got arced in one spot near the hook. Can we just cut that section off and keep running the rest of the rope?

question: If we cut a kinked spot out of the hoist rope, can we splice the two pieces back together? And if we just use the longer piece, is there a minimum number of wraps that has to stay on the drum?

question: During the shift inspection, a competent person notes significant corrosion on a hoist rope. Is the rope automatically removed from service, or is a determination required first?
gold_answer: Removal is not automatic: significant corrosion is a Category I deficiency, so the competent person must immediately determine whether it is a safety hazard. question: Tower crane is set up downtown and we can't get an assist crane in to do the full annual rope inspection. How long can that be put off for the running ropes vs the standing ropes?

question: can a derrick use fiber core rope on the boom hoist

question: We want to run rotation resistant rope on a load hoist that's acting as the boom hoist for a luffing jib on our crawler. What are the drum and sheave size requirements and the minimum design factor for that setup?

question: what's the lowest design factor allowed on rotation resistant rope, and if a type II rope is under 5 for a one-off lift what extra stuff do we have to do

question: for the daily rope check do i have to boom down and open up the rope

question: putting a clip on the wedge socket, which side does it go on, live end or tail?

question: horn on the rig quit this morning, can we just run hand signals and keep a air horn in the cab til the part comes in?

question: Does a crane sitting on a barge need a crane level indicator?

question: how long we got to fix the anti two block once it goes bad

question: A2B is out on our 2005 hydro cherry picker, what's the workaround while we wait on parts

question: boom hoist limit switch is shot what are my options to keep running

question: outrigger sensor on the new machine keeps faulting what now

question: We've got a digger derrick built in 2009 with no anti two block on it. Does it have to have one?

question: Mid-pick the level indicator goes dead, and on another job the boom length indicator goes dead mid-pick. Same deal for both? Can either one keep going?

question: Where the manufacturer's operating procedures for a crane cannot be obtained, who is required to develop the replacement procedures for the controls and for capacity?

question: Mid-shift the display in the cab goes black and that's the only place our load charts are, there's no paper copy. What am I supposed to do?

question: nobody knows what this thing weighs. what are my options for checking it before the pick, and what happens if the LMI shows it's heavy
gold_answer: The operator can get the weight from an industry-recognized source (such as the manufacturer), an industry-recognized calculation, or other equally reliable means. question: Super wants me to make a pick that's over the chart and says just do it. Can he make me, and can I shut the job down if I think it's unsafe?

question: running a locomotive crane in the rail yard, when am I allowed to swing out over the next track over
